claim: The Classic data pointer advances by one after every instruction. Measured on a real image and verified against the oracle's own semantics: a '* < * < v' recipe printed rot(mem[d]) then rot(mem[d+2]) -- exactly the values the pointer-advance rule predicts, the second read landing on d+2 because the print between the two rotations also advances the pointer.

semantics_source.lines: 93-97 (c and d advance after every instruction), 76-79 (op 39 ROT), 82-84 (op 62 CRAZY)

verified_trace.note: the second read lands on d+2, not d+1, because the print between the two rotations also advances the pointer

consequence_for_a_stored_program_loader: The pointer advances, so writing to CONSECUTIVE cells is expressible: a chain of writes lands on d, d+1, d+2, ...

But the only two writing opcodes are op 39 (mem[d] = rot(mem[d])) and op 62 (mem[d] = crz(a, mem[d])). Neither writes an arbitrary value: op 39 can only rotate what is already there, and op 62 mixes the new value with the existing one.

Therefore a byte-exact loader of arbitrary stdin bytes is not expressible as a fixed rectilinear recipe: for each byte X one would need a = find_a_for_crazy(current content, X), and that transformation depends on X, so the recipe would have to vary per input value.
This is a semantic limit of the emitter's opcode set, not a budget limit.
